transcript.text: Determinants of Demand
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift demand left or right.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Demand shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Demand increases and shifts right when buyers want more at every price; demand decreases and shifts left when they want less at every price. Important determinants include income, tastes and preferences, expectations, the number of buyers, and the prices of substitutes and complements. The direction of an income effect depends on whether the good is normal or inferior, and the effect of a related-good price depends on whether the goods are substitutes or complements.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Consumer income, preferences, expectations, or the number of buyers changes.
The price of a substitute or complement changes.
Quantity demanded changes at the same price.
The entire demand curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a demand shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A nonprice determinant changes how much buyers want at every price and shifts the entire curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: DEMAND SHIFT

Horizontal axis: quantity of coffee in thousands. Vertical axis: price of coffee in dollars. Two parallel coffee demand curves. D1 lies to the right of D0; at price $10, quantity demanded rises from 50 thousand on D0 to 125 thousand on D1.

At a coffee price of $10, the original curve D0 shows quantity demanded of 50 thousand, while D1 shows 125 thousand. The price of coffee is held constant, so the 75-thousand increase cannot be a movement along D0. It is a rightward shift from D0 to D1, meaning a nonprice determinant has increased demand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Income rises for buyers of a normal good. Which direction does its demand curve shift, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Determinants of Supply
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-15
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify nonprice determinants that shift supply left or right.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Supply shifts when a nonprice determinant changes. Supply increases and shifts right when sellers can provide more at every price; supply decreases and shifts left when they provide less at every price. Important determinants include input and resource costs, technology and productivity, taxes and subsidies, expectations, the number of sellers, and natural or regulatory production conditions. A change that lowers marginal production cost generally increases supply, while a change that raises marginal cost generally decreases it.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Input prices, technology, productivity, taxes, or subsidies change.
Producers' expectations or the number of sellers changes.
Quantity supplied changes at the same price.
The entire supply curve moves left or right rather than moving to another point on one curve.
WATCH OUT

Do not treat a change in the good's own price as a supply shifter. Own-price changes create movements along the existing curve. A change in production cost, technology, expectations, or the number of sellers changes how much firms offer at every price and shifts the curve.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SUPPLY SHIFT

Horizontal axis: quantity of hamburgers in thousands. Vertical axis: price of hamburgers in dollars. Two parallel hamburger supply curves. S1 lies to the left of S0; at price $9, quantity supplied falls from 200 thousand on S0 to 100 thousand on S1.

At a hamburger price of $9, the original curve S0 shows quantity supplied of 200 thousand, while S1 shows 100 thousand. The product's price is unchanged, so the 100-thousand decrease is not a movement along S0. It is a leftward shift from S0 to S1, consistent with a determinant such as higher input costs reducing supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
A new technology lowers the cost of producing solar panels. Which direction does supply shift, and why?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Market Equilibrium
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-16
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At that price, buyers can purchase the amount they want and sellers can sell the amount they offer, so there is no pressure for price to change. A demand or supply shift creates a new intersection and can change both equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Find the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
On a graph, use the intersection of the demand and supply curves.
A price below equilibrium creates a shortage; a price above equilibrium creates a surplus.
Report both the equilibrium price and the corresponding equilibrium quantity.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to call any intersection or stated price an equilibrium. Equilibrium occurs only where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING MARKET EQUILIBRIUM

The horizontal axis is quantity of gas in thousands and the vertical axis is price of gas. Original demand D0 and original supply S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand. Demand shifts right to D1 while supply shifts left to S1. D1 and S1 intersect at price $5 and quantity 150 thousand. Holding S0 fixed, D1 intersects S0 at price $4 and quantity 200 thousand. Holding D0 fixed, S1 intersects D0 at price $4 and quantity 100 thousand.

On the graph, the new demand and supply curves intersect at a price of $5 and quantity of 150 thousand. The intersection is the only point at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so it is the new market equilibrium. A price above $5 would create a surplus, while a price below $5 would create a shortage.
CHECK YOURSELF
Holding supply constant, which equilibrium outcome follows from an increase in demand?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Simultaneous Shifts
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-18
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Determine equilibrium, shortages, surpluses, adjustment, and comparative statics.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

When demand and supply shift at the same time, each shift contributes separately to the new equilibrium. Analyze how each change affects price and quantity, then combine the directional effects. If both shifts push one variable in the same direction, that result is determinate; if they push in opposite directions, the result depends on the relative size of the shifts.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Both a demand determinant and a supply determinant change.
A bicycle endorsement raises demand while higher input costs reduce supply.
Analyze each shift separately before combining its price and quantity effects.
Opposing effects on one variable leave its direction ambiguous unless relative shift sizes are known.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts. A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
WORKED EXAMPLE: COMBINING DEMAND AND SUPPLY SHIFTS

The horizontal axis is quantity of gas in thousands and the vertical axis is price of gas. Original demand D0 and original supply S0 intersect at price $3 and quantity 150 thousand. Demand shifts right to D1 while supply shifts left to S1. D1 and S1 intersect at price $5 and quantity 150 thousand. Holding S0 fixed, D1 intersects S0 at price $4 and quantity 200 thousand. Holding D0 fixed, S1 intersects D0 at price $4 and quantity 100 thousand.

The original curves D0 and S0 intersect at a price of $3 and quantity of 150 thousand. After demand shifts right to D1 and supply shifts left to S1, the new intersection is $5 and the same quantity of 150 thousand. Both shifts raise price; their opposing quantity effects happen to offset in this graph, though quantity would otherwise be ambiguous.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which pair of market changes is shown when the graph moves from D0/S0 to D1/S1?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
International Trade: Tariffs
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-24
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze International Trade: Tariffs.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price. Domestic firms respond by producing more, consumers buy less, and imports fall. Consumers lose surplus, domestic producers gain surplus, and the government collects tariff revenue. The tariff also prevents mutually beneficial trades, creating deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Begin with an importing country whose world price is below the domestic no-trade price.
Add the tariff per unit to the world price to find the tariff-inclusive domestic price.
At that higher price, read domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied; imports equal their difference.
Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the number of units imported.
Look for lower consumer surplus, higher producer surplus, government revenue, and deadweight loss from overproduction and underconsumption.
WATCH OUT
Do not treat tariff revenue as full welfare loss. Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING TARIFF REVENUE

The horizontal axis is quantity of phone cases and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at point e, price $8 and quantity 150 thousand. Horizontal lines mark world price $4 and domestic price with tariff $6. At $4, supply is 50 thousand and demand is 250 thousand; at $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

At the $4 world price, domestic quantity demanded is 250 thousand and domestic quantity supplied is 50 thousand, so free-trade imports are 200 thousand. A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $6; quantity demanded falls to 200 thousand and quantity supplied rises to 100 thousand. Imports fall to 100 thousand, and government tariff revenue is $2 x 100 thousand = $200 thousand.
CHECK YOURSELF
Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
International Trade: Quotas
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-25
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Analyze International Trade: Quotas.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

An import quota directly limits the quantity of a good that may enter the country. A binding quota reduces imports below their free-trade level, raises the domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption. The price gap between the domestic quota price and the world price creates quota rent. Who receives that rent affects the country's national-surplus result, while the production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Begin with the free-trade outcome at the world price.
A binding import quota limits imports below their free-trade quantity.
The restriction raises domestic price, increases domestic production, and reduces domestic consumption.
The gap between the quota price and world price creates quota rent on each permitted import.
Look for deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume quota rent automatically becomes government revenue. It accrues to whoever holds the import rights; auctioning those rights can transfer the rent to government. The recipient matters for national welfare, while production and consumption distortions create deadweight loss.
WORKED EXAMPLE: QUOTA PRICE AND IMPORTS

The horizontal axis is quantity of phone cases and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at price $7 and quantity 175 thousand. Horizontal lines mark world price $3 and domestic price under quota $6. At $3, supply is 75 thousand and demand is 275 thousand; at $6, supply is 150 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

Before trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at a price of $7. With free trade, buyers can purchase at the $3 world price, which creates imports. The quota limits imports, so the domestic price rises to $6. The difference between the $6 quota price and the $3 world price is $3 per imported unit; that $3 gap is quota rent.
CHECK YOURSELF
A student says equivalent tariffs and quotas remain identical after demand changes. What is the key difference?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Fiscal Policy and Aggregate Demand
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-30
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Trace government purchases and taxes into aggregate demand.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand through changes in government purchases, taxes, and their effects on consumption. Lower purchases and higher taxes both push aggregate demand left. After the first-round spending change, the multiplier process traces additional income-consumption rounds; crowding out can then reduce the net effect. A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Higher government purchases directly raise aggregate demand; lower purchases reduce it.
Tax changes affect aggregate demand indirectly by changing disposable income and consumption.
Expansionary fiscal policy shifts aggregate demand right; contractionary policy shifts it left.
Distinguish a shift of aggregate demand from a movement along the curve caused by the price level.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to classify fiscal policy from the economy's condition rather than the government's action. Higher purchases or lower taxes are expansionary; lower purchases or higher taxes are contractionary.
WORKED EXAMPLE: SHIFTING AGGREGATE DEMAND

The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

At the displayed price level P, an expansionary fiscal action shifts aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2. Real output demanded rises from Y1 to Y2 at that fixed price level. A larger action could shift demand to AD3 and quantity demanded to Y3, but the graph does not establish which package is desirable; that depends on the output gap and timing.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why can a tax cut shift aggregate demand to the right in the short run?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Fiscal Multipliers and Crowding Out
MACROECONOMICS
MACRO-31
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate multiplier effects and evaluate crowding out.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A spending or tax change can create a multiplied demand response, while higher interest rates can crowd out part of the expansion. Fiscal policy can shift AD right, the multiplier can push it farther, and crowding out can pull the final effect back. Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise. Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates. In the simple fixed-price model with lump-sum taxes and no import leakage, the spending multiplier is 1 / (1 - MPC), and the tax multiplier is -MPC / (1 - MPC).
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Initial fiscal shift, multiplier expansion, then crowding out offset.
Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.
Crowding out reduces private investment when fiscal expansion raises interest rates.
Crowding out occurs when higher interest rates reduce private investment spending.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to report a gross multiplier effect without subtracting private spending displaced by higher interest rates. Crowding out makes the net demand increase smaller.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MULTIPLIER VERSUS CROWDING OUT

The horizontal axis is real output Y and the vertical axis is the price level P. A horizontal line at price level P crosses three downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves. AD1 intersects at output Y1, AD2 lies to the right and intersects at Y2, and AD3 lies farther right and intersects at Y3, so Y1 is less than Y2, which is less than Y3.

With MPC = 0.8, the simple spending multiplier is 5. A $20 billion increase in purchases raises demand by $100 billion before offsets. In the graph, AD1 to AD3 is the gross expansion; crowding out leaves AD2. At fixed P, real output demanded rises to Y2 rather than Y3. Actual equilibrium output also depends on aggregate supply.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why might a tax cut have a smaller immediate effect than an equal increase in government purchases?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Price Elasticity of Demand
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-04
Time: 6 minutes
Outcome: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand and interpret the result
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change: PED = absolute percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. The midpoint method uses the average of the two quantities and the average of the two prices, so reversing the direction gives the same result. Demand is elastic when PED is greater than 1, unit elastic at 1, and inelastic below 1. Elasticity uses percentages, not raw unit changes or visual slope. Close substitutes, a longer adjustment period, a larger budget share, and a narrower market definition generally make demand more elastic.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Two price-quantity points are provided for a midpoint calculation.
The problem asks whether the quantity response is elastic, unit elastic, or inelastic.
Substitutes, time to adjust, budget share, or market scope are changing.
A linear demand curve has constant slope but different elasticity along the line.
A horizontal or vertical demand curve represents a limiting elasticity case.
WATCH OUT

A steeper-looking curve is not automatically less elastic. Slope uses the original price and quantity units, while elasticity compares percentage changes and depends on the price-quantity location. Put percentage quantity change in the numerator, use midpoint averages in both denominators, and classify demand using the absolute value of PED.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MIDPOINT ELASTICITY

Price elasticity of demand. Vertical axis: Price, from 0 to 20. Horizontal axis: Quantity, from 0 to 150. The straight downward Demand curve runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Labeled points are C at quantity 30 and price 12, B at quantity 60 and price 8, and A at quantity 90 and price 4. Dashed guides connect each point to its axis values. C to B supplies the worked example; B to A supplies the self-check.

Between C and B, price falls from $12 to $8 while quantity demanded rises from 30 to 60. Using midpoint values, quantity changes by 66.7% and price changes by 40.0%, so PED = 66.7% / 40.0% = 1.67. Because 1.67 is greater than 1, demand is elastic over this interval: quantity responds proportionally more than price changes.
CHECK YOURSELF
Using points B (P = $8, Q = 60) and A (P = $4, Q = 90), what is midpoint PED, and how should demand be classified over that interval?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Elasticity and Total Revenue
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-08
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Connect Elasticity and Total Revenue.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity, and the effect of a price change depends on demand elasticity. A point on demand supplies the price and quantity needed to calculate revenue. At unit elasticity the price and quantity percentage effects offset, marking the revenue peak on a standard linear demand curve.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Calculate total revenue as price multiplied by quantity at each relevant point.
If price and total revenue move in opposite directions, demand is elastic over that range.
If price and total revenue move in the same direction, demand is inelastic over that range.
At unit elasticity, a small price change leaves total revenue approximately unchanged.
WATCH OUT

A common mistake is to compute elasticity without checking the associated total-revenue change. With elastic demand, price and total revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.
WORKED EXAMPLE: ELASTICITY AND REVENUE

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. A straight downward-sloping Demand line runs from price 16 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 120. Its marked points are C at quantity 30, price 12; B at quantity 60, price 8; and A at quantity 90, price 4. Dashed guides show each point on both axes.

At point C, price is $12 and quantity is 30, so total revenue is $12 x 30 = $360. At point B, price is $8 and quantity is 60, so revenue is $480. Moving from C to B lowers price but raises total revenue by $120, indicating elastic demand over that segment.
CHECK YOURSELF
For luxury cruise cabins, price changes from $3200 to $2880 while quantity demanded changes from 1,500 to 1,900. Use the midpoint method and the observed revenue totals. Which statement is correct?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-10
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Consumer Surplus & Willingness to Pay.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Consumer surplus is the difference between a buyer's willingness to pay and the price actually paid. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Demand can be interpreted as buyers' marginal willingness to pay. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a buyer's willingness to pay and the market price actually paid.
Individual consumer surplus equals willingness to pay minus price.
On a graph, consumer surplus is the area below demand and above the market price up to the quantity traded.
A buyer whose willingness to pay is below price does not purchase and earns no consumer surplus.
WATCH OUT
Do not assume every trade creates surplus. The gain from an additional trade is the buyer’s willingness to pay minus the seller’s cost, not either side’s individual surplus alone.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING CONSUMER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.

At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The demand intercept of $30 represents the highest willingness to pay. Consumer surplus is the triangle above price and below demand: 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the rectangle below market price not consumer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-11
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Explain Producer Surplus & Willingness to Accept.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Producer surplus is the difference between the price a seller receives and the seller's willingness to accept. Surplus analysis compares value created with the opportunity cost of the resources used. Producer surplus is the price-cost gap across units supplied. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for a seller's willingness to accept or marginal cost and the price received.
Individual producer surplus equals price received minus willingness to accept.
On a graph, producer surplus is the area above supply and below the market price up to the quantity traded.
A seller whose cost exceeds the market price does not make that trade.
WATCH OUT
Do not confuse wta price gap. Producer surplus measures the price received above the seller’s willingness to accept for that unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING PRODUCER SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
At equilibrium, price is $14 and quantity is 8. The supply intercept is $6, so producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why is the full area above supply not producer surplus?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-12
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Total Surplus & Gains from Exchange.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Total surplus equals consumer surplus plus producer surplus and measures the gains created by exchange. Each trade adds to total surplus when the buyer's willingness to pay exceeds the seller's opportunity cost. Total surplus is maximized when every mutually beneficial trade occurs and no trade with a cost above its value is completed.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Add consumer surplus and producer surplus to obtain total surplus.
For each possible trade, compare the buyer's willingness to pay with the seller's opportunity cost.
A trade creates gains when buyer value exceeds seller cost.
On a graph, total surplus is the area between demand and supply up to the quantity traded.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to fail to separate transfer from total loss. Consumer surplus is $10 and producer surplus is $8; their sum equals the $18 gain from exchange.
WORKED EXAMPLE: CALCULATING TOTAL SURPLUS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 30, and upward-sloping S starts at price 6. They meet at E, quantity 8 and price 14. Dashed guides connect E to both axes. The demand segment above price 14 runs from quantity 0 to 8; the supply segment below price 14 runs over that same quantity interval.
The graph's equilibrium is 8 units at $14. Consumer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($30 - $14) = $64, and producer surplus is 1/2 x 8 x ($14 - $6) = $32. Total surplus is therefore $64 + $32 = $96.
CHECK YOURSELF
Buyer value is $17 and seller cost is $22. Efficient action?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Efficient Quantity & Allocation
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-13
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Identify Efficient Quantity & Allocation.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The efficient quantity includes every unit whose buyer value is at least as large as its opportunity cost. Efficiency pairs the highest-value buyers with the lowest-cost sellers and continues exchange while the next buyer's willingness to pay covers the next seller's cost. Producing beyond that point destroys surplus, while stopping before it leaves gains unrealized.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Order potential trades from the highest buyer value and the lowest seller cost.
Complete every trade for which willingness to pay is at least as large as opportunity cost.
Stop when the next seller's cost exceeds the next buyer's value.
An efficient allocation sends the good to the highest-value buyers and production to the lowest-cost sellers.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to equate more output with more efficiency. The forced extra unit contributes $23 - $29 = -$6 to total surplus.
WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING THE EFFICIENT QUANTITY

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Downward-sloping D starts at price 18 at quantity 0 and reaches price 2 at quantity 16. Upward-sloping S starts at price 2 and reaches price 18 at quantity 16. They intersect at E, quantity 8 and price 10, with dashed guides to the axes. Demand lies above supply to the left of E and below supply to its right.

Demand and supply intersect at 8 units and $10. At that quantity, the marginal buyer's value equals the marginal seller's cost. Units below 8 create positive gains from trade; units above 8 cost more than buyers value them. The efficient allocation therefore produces 8 units.
CHECK YOURSELF

Five buyers each want one studio pass, with willingness-to-pay values [27, 23, 18, 13, 8]. Five sellers can each supply one, with costs [4, 10, 15, 21, 25]. Ignore any announced market price. Rank buyers from highest to lowest value and sellers from lowest to highest cost. Which statement correctly identifies the efficient cutoff?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-17
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Gains from Trade, Surplus & Winners/Losers.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

International trade changes consumer and producer surplus and creates net gains when the world price differs from the no-trade equilibrium price. The surplus framework converts distributional changes into a net total-surplus comparison. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers.
The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
Higher export prices redistribute surplus toward producers while creating a positive net gain in the standard model.
Aggregate gains do not imply universal gains.
WATCH OUT

Do not assume trade has only winners or only losers. Trade creates net gains while redistributing surplus between buyers and sellers. The efficiency result is based on the net change in combined surplus, not on every group winning.
WORKED EXAMPLE: TRACING TRADE WINNERS AND LOSERS

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: price. Demand D falls from price 80 at quantity 0 to price 0 at quantity 80. Supply S rises from price 20 and crosses D at quantity 30 and price 50. The horizontal world-price line Pw at price 30 meets S at quantity 10 and D at quantity 50; dashed vertical guides mark both quantities.

At the $30 world price, domestic producers supply 10 units and domestic consumers demand 50, so imports equal 40. Relative to the $50 no-trade equilibrium, the two gain-from-trade triangles each have base 20 and height 20. Their combined area is $200 + $200 = $400.
CHECK YOURSELF
Why do consumers gain when a lower world price opens an import market?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-22
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Average Costs: AFC, AVC & ATC.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Average fixed cost, average variable cost, and average total cost express costs per unit of output. Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost. Average fixed cost falls as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units, while average variable cost changes with the productivity and price of variable inputs.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Divide fixed cost by output for average fixed cost and variable cost by output for average variable cost.
Average total cost equals average fixed cost plus average variable cost.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output spreads the same fixed cost across more units.
Use per-unit measures only when output is positive.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to misuse average cost formula. AVC = $300/20 = $15; AFC = $5; ATC = $20. TVC = $1,000; AVC = $20, AFC = $8, and ATC = $28.
WORKED EXAMPLE: READING AVERAGE-COST CURVES

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

At 400 units, the graph shows average cost of $20 and average variable cost of $12. Because AC = AVC + AFC, average fixed cost is $20 - $12 = $8 per unit. The gap between AC and AVC is therefore the firm's average fixed cost.
CHECK YOURSELF
Cost schedule 2: At Q=29, Ironwood Furniture has AVC=$13.97 and ATC=$24.31. What fixed-cost conclusion follows?
READY?
Return to the game and master this concept.
Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-23
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Calculate Marginal Cost & Production-Cost Linkages.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

Marginal cost is the change in total cost caused by producing one more unit. Divide the input cost by marginal product. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Look for the change in total cost caused by producing one additional unit.
Compute marginal cost as the change in total cost divided by the change in output.
A fixed-cost change does not change marginal cost, but a variable-input cost change usually does.
When marginal product falls, marginal cost tends to rise if the input price is unchanged.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to move mp and mc together. Higher MP lowers variable input cost per extra unit. A constant addition to cost at every output does not change the cost of producing one more unit.
WORKED EXAMPLE: LINKING MARGINAL PRODUCT AND COST

Horizontal axis: quantity; vertical axis: costs in dollars. Curves are labeled MC, AC and AVC. MC first dips slightly and then rises. It crosses AVC at its minimum, quantity 200 and cost 10. At quantity 400, MC crosses AC at its minimum of 20, while AVC is 12. Dashed guides mark the quantities and costs. AC remains above AVC.

Marginal cost crosses AVC at AVC's minimum of $10 and 200 units, then crosses AC at AC's minimum of $20 and 400 units. When marginal cost is below an average, it pulls that average down; when marginal cost rises above it, the average begins to increase.

THE CORE IDEA

Short-run cost curves move differently because fixed costs affect AFC and ATC, while variable-input costs affect AVC, ATC, and MC. A below-average marginal observation pulls the average down. Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.
A technology improvement reduces the variable input needed at every output.
Labor is the variable input in the standard short-run model.
A firm receives a property-tax increase that does not depend on output.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to mix fixed and variable shifts. A fixed-cost increase raises fixed cost per unit and total cost per unit but leaves variable and marginal cost unchanged.

A cartel coordinates firms to restrict industry output and raise price as a monopolist would. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome. Individual incentives can push both firms toward a lower-payoff noncooperative outcome.
The conflict is between individual and collective incentives.
A prisoner’s dilemma exists precisely because individual incentives can undermine a jointly better outcome.
Three firms agree to keep prices high.

Do not miss individual incentive to defect. The conflict is between individual and collective incentives. Private incentives can conflict with the cartel’s collective restriction.

Externalities
MICROECONOMICS
MICRO-54
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Compare private and social incentives and identify the efficient quantity.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

An externality is a cost or benefit imposed on someone outside a transaction. Negative externalities make private decision makers ignore part of social cost; positive externalities make them ignore part of social benefit. Efficiency uses all marginal social costs and benefits.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Ask whether the spillover is a cost or benefit and whether it comes from production or consumption.
Negative: MSC > MPC or MPB > MSB, so the market quantity is too high.
Positive: MSB > MPB or MPC > MSC, so the market quantity is too low.
Corrective taxes, subsidies, permits, regulation, or bargaining can internalize the spillover.
WATCH OUT
Do not label every harmful outcome an externality. A spillover must affect a third party and be missing from the market price.
WORKED EXAMPLE: NEGATIVE PRODUCTION EXTERNALITY

Negative production externality in fast-fashion garments. Horizontal axis: quantity of garments in millions, with labeled ticks from 40 to 320. Vertical axis: marginal benefit and cost, with labeled dollar ticks from 3 to 24. MPB slopes downward from 21 to 9; MPC slopes upward from 3 to 15; MSC slopes upward from 9 to 21, six dollars above MPC throughout. MPB and MPC intersect at 240 million garments and 12 dollars. MPB and MSC intersect at 160 million garments and 15 dollars. Dashed guides mark both quantities and values.

Fast-fashion production creates a $6 external cost per garment, so MSC lies $6 above MPC. The market produces 240 million garments where MPB = MPC at $12. Efficiency occurs at 160 million garments where MPB = MSC at $15, eliminating 80 million units of overproduction. A $6 corrective tax aligns private and social marginal cost.

Outcome: Classify goods and apply efficient provision and resource-use rules.

THE CORE IDEA

Excludability asks whether nonpayers can be kept out; rivalry asks whether one person's use reduces another's. Public goods are nonexcludable and nonrival, common resources are nonexcludable and rival, club goods are excludable and nonrival, and private goods are excludable and rival.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Free riding can make private payments understate total social willingness to pay for a public good.
Vertically sum individual marginal benefits to obtain MSB for a shared quantity.
Provide the efficient public-good quantity where MSB = MC.
Common resources tend toward overuse; property rights, access rules, or practical exclusion can change incentives.

Do not classify a good by who supplies it. Government provision does not automatically make a good nonexcludable or nonrival.
WORKED EXAMPLE: VERTICAL SUMMATION

Horizontal axis: community fireworks displays per summer; vertical axis: marginal benefit / cost in thousands of dollars per display. Dashed North MB falls from 50 at zero displays to 30 at four; dashed South MB falls from 40 to 20 at four and reaches zero at eight. Solid MSB is their vertical sum: 90 at zero and 50 at four. Horizontal MC is 50. At four displays, guides mark North 30, South 20 and the MSB-MC intersection at 50. MSB then falls to zero at ten displays.

At four community fireworks displays, North's marginal benefit is $30,000 and South's is $20,000. Because both communities consume the same shared quantity, MSB is the vertical sum: $50,000. MC is also $50,000, so four displays are efficient. Summing quantities horizontally would be incorrect.

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Use a budget constraint and preferences to identify the best affordable bundle.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

A budget constraint shows every bundle a consumer can afford at given income and prices. Its intercepts are income divided by each good's price, and its slope is the negative relative price. Preferences rank feasible bundles; the optimum is the highest attainable indifference curve, usually where MRS equals the price ratio.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Bundles inside or on the budget line are feasible; bundles outside it are infeasible.
An income change shifts the line in parallel when prices are fixed.
A change in one price pivots the line around the unchanged intercept.
At an interior optimum, marginal utility per dollar is equal across goods.
WATCH OUT
Spending the whole budget is not enough to prove optimality. The chosen bundle must also provide the highest attainable preference ranking.

At A the budget line is tangent to solid IC2. Dashed IC1 lies below IC2 and intersects the feasible set; dashed IC3 lies above IC2 and outside the budget line. All three indifference curves slope down and are convex toward the origin.

The budget line reaches 20 units of X or 40 units of Y, so its slope is -2. Bundle A contains 10 units of X and 20 of Y. At A, the budget line is tangent to IC2, the highest attainable indifference curve. IC3 is preferred but lies outside the feasible set, while IC1 is attainable but provides a lower ranking.

THE CORE IDEA

At a world price, domestic consumption is read from demand and domestic production is read from supply. When domestic consumption exceeds domestic production, imports fill the difference; when production exceeds consumption, the excess is exported. The comparison must be made at the world price because that price guides both domestic buyers and sellers under free trade.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the world price with the domestic no-trade equilibrium price.
At the world price, read domestic consumption from demand and domestic production from supply.
When consumption exceeds production, imports equal domestic consumption minus domestic production.
When production exceeds consumption, exports equal domestic production minus domestic consumption.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to omit one or more welfare components. Revenue is tariff×imports; each side distortion is a triangle. Total DWL is $144.

Horizontal axis: quantity of avocados in thousands; vertical axis: price of avocados in dollars. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up. They intersect at A, quantity 175 thousand and price 7. A horizontal world-price line marked Pw = $10 meets demand at 100 thousand and supply at 250 thousand. Dashed vertical guides show those quantities.

Without trade, domestic supply and demand intersect at $7 and 175 thousand avocados. At the $10 world price, domestic consumers buy 100 thousand while domestic producers supply 250 thousand. The country exports the difference: 250 - 100 = 150 thousand avocados.
